# UI and accessibility

- UI-001 (should): Every UI an app ships meets WCAG 2.2 level AA: web UI (Blazor, Razor) as written, native UI (MAUI, desktop) as W3C's WCAG2ICT note applies it. Building UI, an agent checks at least the success criteria UI-003 lists, keeping each one's own exceptions, such as a link inside a sentence or a data table that needs two dimensions.
- UI-003 (should): For WCAG 2.2 level AA conformance, a UI satisfies all the level A and level AA success criteria (or a level AA conforming alternate version is provided); among them, each with the exceptions and conditions WCAG lists: non-text content has a text alternative, and non-text content that is a control or accepts user input has a name that describes its purpose (1.1.1); information, structure and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text (1.3.1); color isn't the only visual means of conveying information (1.4.1); text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and large-scale text at least 3:1 (1.4.3); text, except captions and images of text, can be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality (1.4.4); vertically scrolling content can be presented at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels without loss of information or functionality and without scrolling in two dimensions (1.4.10); the visual information required to identify user interface components and states has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors (1.4.11); all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface (2.1.1), and focus moved to a component with the keyboard can be moved away with the keyboard (2.1.2); where navigation sequences affect meaning or operation, components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability (2.4.3); keyboard operable UI has a mode where the focus indicator is visible (2.4.7), and a component receiving focus isn't entirely hidden by author-created content (2.4.11); pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (2.5.8); labels or instructions are provided when content requires user input (3.3.2); no step in authentication requires a cognitive function test unless that step provides an alternative or a mechanism WCAG lists (3.3.8); and every user interface component's name and role can be programmatically determined (4.1.2). W3C's WCAG2ICT note helps clarify how to use WCAG 2 for non-web software.
